per_question.question: What DME items are specifically NOT covered by NC Medicaid under the Orthotics and Prosthetics policy, and what general criteria must be met for coverage?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under NC Medicaid Clinical Coverage Policy 5B, the **specific items/devices not covered** are:

- **Devices for the beneficiary’s comfort or convenience**, or for the convenience of the beneficiary’s caregiver
- **Backup devices** or **duplicate devices** kept at different locations
- **Devices and supplies for residents of nursing facilities**
- **Devices or supplies covered by another agency**
- **Equipment or supplies for beneficiaries receiving hospice care**  
  ([Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), § 4.2.1)

There are also **general not-covered rules**. Orthotics/prosthetics are not covered if:

- The beneficiary does **not meet the eligibility requirements in Section 2.0**
- The beneficiary does **not meet the coverage criteria in Section 3.0**
- The item/service **duplicates another provider’s** procedure, product, or service
- The item/service is **experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial**  
  ([Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), § 4.1)

## General criteria that must be met for coverage

For coverage, the policy requires that orthotic or prosthetic items:

- Be **ordered by a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner**
- Be **medically necessary** to maintain or improve the beneficiary’s medical, physical, or functional level
- Be **appropriate for use in a noninstitutional setting** where normal life activities occur
- Be supported by a **documented face-to-face encounter** related to the primary reason for the device, occurring **no more than 6 months before** initiation
- Have the beneficiary’s need **reviewed at least annually** by the ordering physician, PA, or NP  
  ([Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), § 3.2.1)

The policy also says the device must be:

- A **reasonable and medically necessary part of the treatment plan**
- **Consistent with the beneficiary’s diagnosis and medical condition**, especially functional limitations and symptoms
- **Of high quality**, with replacement parts available and obtainable  
  ([Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), § 3.2.1)

## Additional medical-necessity standards

The policy further explains:

- **Orthotic devices** are medically necessary when needed to **correct or prevent skeletal deformities**, **support or align movable body parts**, or **preserve or improve physical function**
- **Prosthetic devices** are medically necessary as a **replacement for all or part of the function** of a permanently inoperative, absent, or malfunctioning body part, and the beneficiary must need the prosthesis for **mobility, daily care, or rehabilitation**  
  ([Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), § 3.2.1)

## Bottom line

NC Medicaid covers orthotics and prosthetics under Policy 5B only when the item is properly ordered, medically necessary, clinically appropriate, supported by recent face-to-face documentation, and not excluded by the policy. It does **not** cover convenience items, backup/duplicate devices, nursing-facility devices/supplies, items covered by another agency, hospice-related equipment/supplies, duplicative services, or experimental/investigational items.  
Current authoritative document checked: [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment) (no amendment returned by the amendment record query).

per_question.question: What are the entrance, continued service, and discharge criteria for outpatient behavioral health services in NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
For NC Medicaid outpatient behavioral health services, the policy sets specific **entrance, continued service, and discharge criteria** in Clinical Coverage Policy **8C**, effective **April 15, 2025**.

## Entrance criteria
A beneficiary meets entrance criteria when all of the following are present:

- a current **DSM-5** diagnosis;
- behavioral, psychological, or biological dysfunction and functional impairment consistent with and associated with that diagnosis;
- if a higher level of care is indicated but unavailable, or the beneficiary refuses it, outpatient services may be provided until that higher level is available or to support the beneficiary’s participation in that higher level of care;
- the beneficiary is capable of developing skills to manage symptoms, make behavioral changes, and respond favorably to therapeutic interventions; and
- there is no evidence that alternative interventions would be more effective under North Carolina community practice standards.  
  [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment), § 3.2.1.1 (effective 2025-04-15)

## Continued service criteria
For continued services, the policy requires:

### First, at least one of these:
- the desired outcome or level of functioning has not been restored, improved, or sustained within the timeframe in the treatment plan;
- the beneficiary continues to be at risk for relapse based on current clinical assessment and history; or
- gains are tenuous.

### And, in addition, at least one of these:
- the beneficiary has achieved current treatment-plan goals, but additional goals are indicated by documented symptoms; or
- the beneficiary is making satisfactory progress toward meeting goals, with documentation supporting that progress.  
  [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment), § 3.2.1.2 (effective 2025-04-15)

## Discharge criteria
Discharge is appropriate when any of the following applies:

- the beneficiary’s level of functioning has improved with respect to the goals in the treatment plan;
- the beneficiary or legally responsible person no longer wants the services; or
- despite modifications to the treatment plan, the beneficiary has not shown improvement and needs a more appropriate best-practice or evidence-based treatment modality under North Carolina community practice standards.  
  [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment), § 3.2.1.3 (effective 2025-04-15)

## Documentation note
The provider’s record must include documentation of the **entrance criteria, continued service criteria, and discharge criteria**.  
[8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment), § 7.3.1 (effective 2025-04-15)

per_question.question: How does the EPSDT special provision affect coverage for outpatient therapy services, and what ordering practitioner requirements apply to beneficiaries under 21?
per_question.agent_answer:
For beneficiaries under 21, the EPSDT special provision can expand coverage for outpatient therapy services beyond ordinary policy limits when the service is medically necessary to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or condition. But EPSDT does **not** waive prior approval requirements. And the therapy still must be ordered before services begin by an approved ordering practitioner. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)]

## Effect of EPSDT on outpatient therapy coverage

Clinical Coverage Policy 10A includes an **EPSDT Special Provision: Exception to Policy Limitations for a Medicaid Beneficiary under 21 Years of Age**. That provision cites 42 U.S.C. § 1396d(r) and indicates EPSDT does not allow coverage for services that are **unsafe, ineffective, experimental/investigational, not medical in nature, or not generally recognized as accepted medical practice or treatment**. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 2.2.1]

For outpatient therapy specifically, the policy also states that if a service, product, or procedure requires **prior approval**, being under 21 **does not eliminate** that requirement. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), “b. EPSDT and Prior Approval Requirements”]

So, in practical terms:

- **EPSDT may broaden coverage** for medically necessary outpatient therapy for a beneficiary under 21.
- **EPSDT does not remove prior authorization/prior approval rules** where the policy requires them.
- The service still must satisfy the policy’s medical-necessity standards and cannot be covered if it is unsafe, experimental/investigational, not medical in nature, or not generally accepted. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 2.2.1; “b. EPSDT and Prior Approval Requirements”]

## Ordering practitioner requirements for beneficiaries under 21

Policy 10A’s **Ordering Practitioners** section lists the practitioners who may order services:

- Medical Doctor (MD)
- Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine (DO)
- Doctor of Podiatric Medicine (DPM)
- Certified Nurse Midwife (CNM)
- Physician Assistant (PA)
- Nurse Practitioner (NP) [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 3.1.2]

For treatment services, the policy further requires that:

- **A verbal or written order must be obtained before services start**;
- verbal orders must document the date and signature of the person receiving the order, be recorded in the beneficiary’s health record, and be **countersigned by the physician within 60 calendar days**;
- verbal orders are valid for **up to six months** from the documented receipt date;
- written orders are valid for **up to six months** from the physician signature date; and
- **backdating is not allowed**. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), treatment-service requirements section]

## Therapy-specific documentation for children and youth

For speech-language therapy, the policy has pediatric criteria specifically applicable to beneficiaries **under 21 years of age**. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 3.2.1.3]

For audiology/aural rehabilitation, coverage requires medically necessary audiology services and documented deficits/functional limitations, including measurable functional limitations identified by the provider. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 3.2.1.4]

Also, for beneficiaries under 21, Policy 10A provides medical-necessity visit guidelines for speech-language and audiology therapy based on severity, with visits limited to the medically necessary number within an authorization period not exceeding six calendar months. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 5.4]

## Bottom line

For a beneficiary under 21, EPSDT can support coverage of medically necessary outpatient therapy even when ordinary policy limits might otherwise restrict it, **but it does not eliminate prior approval requirements**. The therapy must still be properly ordered before treatment begins, and the ordering practitioner must be one of the practitioner types listed in Policy 10A. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), §§ 2.2.1, 3.1.2, 3.2.1.3, 3.2.1.4, 5.4; “b. EPSDT and Prior Approval Requirements”]

I checked amendments for Policy 10A and found no listed amendments; the policy document returned as current has an effective date of **February 1, 2025**.

per_question.question: Does NC Medicaid cover Personal Care Services for beneficiaries who live in an assisted living facility?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes — NC Medicaid does cover Personal Care Services for some beneficiaries who live in an assisted living–type setting, but only if they meet the congregate-setting PCS eligibility criteria.

Under NC Medicaid’s congregate-setting PCS policy, coverage applies when the beneficiary lives in a qualifying licensed congregate facility, including an Adult Care Home or certain licensed group homes, and also meets the medical/functional criteria for PCS. Those criteria include specified unmet needs with activities of daily living, medical linkage to the needed PCS, physician oversight, and the requirement that the person be medically stable and not need continuous licensed nursing care. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings, § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

If those criteria are met, Medicaid covers PCS such as hands-on help with qualifying ADLs, related cueing or prompting, certain related IADLs, medication assistance tied to the condition, help with adaptive equipment or durable medical equipment, and certain special assistance tasks. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings, § 3.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

But Medicaid does **not** cover everything associated with assisted living. The policy specifically excludes, among other things, skilled nursing, transportation, respite, companion sitting, ongoing supervision/monitoring, and **room and board**. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings, § 4.2.1.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

So the short answer is: **yes, PCS can be covered in an assisted living facility, but not the assisted living facility’s room-and-board charges, and only for beneficiaries who satisfy the policy’s congregate-setting PCS requirements.**

per_question.question: Can a CAP/DA beneficiary transfer between service providers, and what rules govern transfers of eligible beneficiaries?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. A CAP/DA beneficiary can transfer, and the governing rule is the CAP/DA policy’s transfer section.

## CAP/DA transfer rule

Under **Section 3.3, “Transfers of Eligible Beneficiaries,”** the **CME must coordinate the transfer to prevent gaps in services**. Before the transfer, the policy requires these steps:

- determine the anticipated service start date;
- coordinate a transition plan between provider agencies;
- discuss and plan for the beneficiary’s health, safety, and well-being;
- initiate transfer of the electronic health record in the CAP Business System (e-CAP/DA) to the receiving county;
- arrange a home visit within **5 business days** after the beneficiary moves to the new primary residence, so the receiving entity can assess the home environment and identify health and welfare concerns; and
- coordinate services so they begin on the **first date of transfer**.  
  [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) (effective Sept. 1, 2025), § 3.3.

## Transfers between counties / agencies

For a **CAP/DA beneficiary transferring to a different county**, Section 3.3 says:

- the transferring CME and receiving CME must coordinate the transfer on the agreed transfer date or **within less than 30 calendar days of the request to transfer**;
- both CMEs must plan for the beneficiary’s health, safety, and well-being;
- the electronic health record must be transferred to the receiving county;
- the receiving CME must arrange the **5-business-day home visit** after the move; and
- services must start on the **first date of the transfer** into the receiving county.  
  [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), § 3.3.

## Related beneficiary/provider rules

The policy also supports beneficiary choice among providers. The CAP/DA person-centered service plan must document the beneficiary’s **right to choose among providers** and among Medicaid-enrolled providers through a signed freedom-of-choice form. That supports the idea that beneficiaries are not locked into one provider, although the specific operational transfer rules are in § 3.3.  
[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), § 5.4.2.

Providers also must respond to service authorizations in e-CAP within **3 business days**, which helps govern how service transitions are implemented.  
[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), § 6.5.

## Federal rule

I could not verify that **42 CFR 413.64** governs beneficiary transfers in CAP/DA. That regulation addresses **provider payment and reimbursement methodology**, not transfer rights or transfer procedures for CAP/DA beneficiaries.  
[42 CFR Part 413](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-413), § 413.64.

## Bottom line

A CAP/DA beneficiary **may transfer**, including when moving to another county, but the transfer must be coordinated by the involved CMEs so there is **no gap in services**, with required planning, record transfer, a prompt home visit, and service start on the transfer date. The main governing source is **CAP/DA Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, § 3.3**.

per_question.question: Is there a maximum earned income limit for people on HCWD (Health Coverage for Workers with Disabilities), and what premiums apply?
per_question.agent_answer:
No—NC Medicaid HCWD does **not** impose a maximum **earned** income limit in the surfaced policy. The policy says HCWD covers individuals “regardless of total countable income,” but there **is** a limit on **unearned** income: people with unearned income **greater than 150% of the Federal Poverty Level (FPL)** are not eligible. [[MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)] [[CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 01-14, HCWD Phase III](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma_cn01-14.pdf)]

## What the policy requires

To qualify for HCWD, a person must be employed and “meet the income requirements for his coverage group,” among other eligibility rules. [[MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)]

The income rule surfaced here is:

- **Unearned income over 150% FPL:** **not eligible** for HCWD.
- **Total countable income at or below 150% FPL:** **no cost sharing** other than applicable co-payments.
- **Total countable income over 150% FPL:** **$50 annual enrollment fee**.
- **Total countable monthly income over 200% FPL:** **monthly premium** is due **in addition to** the $50 annual enrollment fee.
- Premiums rise by income band until income is **over 450% FPL**, when a **full premium** is due. [[MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)] [[CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 01-14, HCWD Phase III](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma_cn01-14.pdf)]

per_question.question: What is the federal statutory authority for NC's CAP/DA waiver, and what does the state need to demonstrate in its waiver application?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC’s CAP/DA waiver is federally authorized as a **Medicaid home- and community-based services waiver under section 1915(c) of the Social Security Act**, as implemented in **42 CFR Part 441, Subpart G**. In the federal regulations governing the waiver request, the state must submit a waiver application that includes the required assurances and documentation, identifies any Medicaid requirements it seeks to waive, and shows that the waiver serves people who would otherwise require an institutional level of care. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) § 441.301; [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) § 441.303.

## Federal governing authority

The controlling federal regulation for the waiver application is **42 CFR § 441.301, “Contents of request for a waiver.”** That section says a waiver request must include:

- the assurances required by **§ 441.302** and the supporting documentation required by **§ 441.303**;
- when applicable, requests to waive Medicaid requirements on:
  - **statewide application** under **section 1902(a)(1)** of the Act,
  - **comparability of services** under **section 1902(a)(10)(B)**, and
  - certain **income and resource rules for medically needy individuals in the community** under **section 1902(a)(10)(C)(i)(III)**;
- a statement whether the agency will refuse HCBS to a beneficiary if the expected cost would exceed the cost of equivalent institutional care; and
- for HCBS waivers, provisions limiting services to people who, without waiver services, would require the Medicaid-covered level of care provided in a hospital, nursing facility, or ICF/IID, as applicable. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) § 441.301.

So, at the federal level, the CAP/DA waiver rests on the **1915(c) HCBS waiver framework**, with application requirements laid out in **42 CFR §§ 441.301 and 441.303**. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441).

## What the state must demonstrate in the waiver application

Under **42 CFR § 441.301**, the state’s application must show, at minimum:

- **Institutional level of care:** beneficiaries served under the waiver would, absent HCBS, require the covered level of care provided in a hospital, nursing facility, or ICF/IID, as applicable.
- **Target group:** the waiver is limited to an allowable target group, including **aged or disabled individuals**, individuals with intellectual/developmental disabilities, or individuals with mental illness. For CAP/DA, the relevant federal target-group category is the **aged or disabled** category. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) § 441.301(b)(1), (6).
- **Defined services:** the application must describe the waiver services separately and specifically; services cannot be left open-ended in scope. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) § 441.301(b)(4).
- **Plan-of-care / person-centered planning structure:** services must be furnished under a written **person-centered service plan** subject to Medicaid agency approval, and the application must describe who is qualified to develop that plan. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) § 441.301(b)(1)(i), (2), (c).
- **Noninstitutional setting:** services are only for beneficiaries who are not inpatients of a hospital, nursing facility, or ICF/IID. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) § 441.301(b)(1)(ii).
- **Evaluation documentation:** the application must provide that the individual evaluation documentation required by **§ 441.303(c)** will be met. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) § 441.301(b)(5).

Under **42 CFR § 441.303**, the state also must furnish supporting documentation showing:

- **health and welfare safeguards** for beneficiaries;
- **financial accountability** records and information;
- a plan for **evaluation and reevaluation** of beneficiaries, including:
  - who performs the evaluations and how,
  - the evaluation form used,
  - procedures for maintaining written evaluation records,
  - procedures for reevaluations at regular intervals;
- how eligible beneficiaries will be informed of **feasible alternatives** and allowed to choose either institutional services or HCBS;
- how post-eligibility income and resource rules will be applied for individuals eligible under a special income level; and
- **cost neutrality**: documentation showing the estimated average per-capita cost under the waiver does **not exceed** the estimated average per-capita cost of care without the waiver. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) § 441.303(a)-(f).

The regulation also requires the state to state the number of **unduplicated beneficiaries** it intends to serve in each year of the waiver program, which functions as a cap unless CMS approves a higher number through amendment. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) § 441.303(f)(6).

That policy reflects the state’s implementation of the federal waiver structure. For example, it identifies CAP/DA participation options and sets general coverage criteria within North Carolina’s program rules. ## Bottom line

For NC’s CAP/DA waiver, the key federal authority is **section 1915(c) of the Social Security Act**, implemented through **42 CFR Part 441**, especially **§ 441.301** and **§ 441.303**. In its waiver application, North Carolina must demonstrate that:

- the waiver serves an allowable target group;

- services are specifically defined and delivered under a person-centered service plan;
- beneficiary health, welfare, choice, and financial accountability are protected;
- evaluations and reevaluations are properly structured and documented; and

per_question.question: How many days of therapeutic leave from a nursing facility does NC Medicaid allow per year, and what conditions must be met?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid allows **up to 60 days of therapeutic leave per calendar year** for an eligible nursing facility resident, subject to specific conditions. No more than **15 consecutive therapeutic leave days** may be taken **without NC Medicaid approval**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment)]

## Conditions that must be met
Under NC Medicaid policy, therapeutic leave must meet these requirements:

- The resident must be **Medicaid-eligible** and occupying a **nursing facility bed for which NC Medicaid is paying reimbursement**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment)]
- The leave must be **for therapeutic purposes only**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment)]
- The leave must be **ordered by the resident’s attending physician**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment)]
- The **necessity for the leave must be documented in the resident’s plan of care**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment)]
- A **therapeutic justification for each instance of leave** must be entered in the resident’s **health record**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment)]

## Additional limits and rules
- The facility must **reserve the resident’s bed** during the therapeutic leave. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment)]
- The facility may not receive any Medicaid revenue for that resident during the absence **other than reimbursement for the reserved bed**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment)]
- Medicaid does **not** reimburse therapeutic leave days that **exceed the legal limit**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment)]
- Therapeutic leave is **not available** if the resident is away for the purpose of receiving **inpatient or nursing services elsewhere**, or at a **different level of care in the current facility**, when those services are paid by Medicaid. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment)]
- Transportation to the therapeutic leave site is **not considered an emergency**, so **ambulance transportation is not reimbursed by Medicaid** for that purpose. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment)]

per_question.question: If a Private Duty Nursing provider terminates services for a Medicaid beneficiary, what notification requirements must they follow?
per_question.agent_answer:
A PDN provider that terminates/discharges services must notify **NC Medicaid within 5 business days** and submit the required discharge paperwork. The exact notice depends on why services are ending.

## Required notification under NC Medicaid PDN policy

Under **Section 5.2.4.1, “Notification of Termination,”** of **[3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment)**:

- **If the PDN provider discharges the beneficiary:**  
  The provider must submit the **DMA-3513 (PDN Discharge Summary Form)** to **NC Medicaid within 5 business days**.

- **If the provider discharges the beneficiary from Medicaid coverage because another source of nursing coverage is available:**  
  The provider must, within **5 business days**:
  - notify **NC Medicaid**,
  - submit the **DMA-3513**, and
  - include:
    - the **last date PDN services were provided and billable to Medicaid**, and
    - the **name of the other source of coverage**.

- **If the attending physician discharges the beneficiary:**  
  The PDN provider must, within **5 business days**, send **NC Medicaid**:
  - the **attending physician’s order terminating PDN services**, and
  - the **DMA-3513 (PDN Discharge Summary Form)**.

## Appeal-related point

The same section states that **the decision of the beneficiary’s attending physician and/or the PDN service provider to discharge the beneficiary cannot be appealed to NC Medicaid**. By contrast, if **NC Medicaid** itself terminates PDN because eligibility, policy criteria, or medical necessity is not met, **NC Medicaid or its designee must send written adverse-notice to the beneficiary/legal representative including appeal rights**. See **Section 5.2.4.1** of **[3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment)**.

## If services stop because of eligibility loss or a long break in care

If PDN ends because the beneficiary **loses NC Medicaid eligibility**, or **no PDN services are provided for 30 consecutive days** for any reason (including hospitalization), the policy says **the prior approval process must be started again**. See **Section 5.2.4.1** of **[3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment)**.

## Federal notice rule

For Medicaid managed care, termination notices are considered written materials critical to obtaining services and must be provided in an understandable and accessible format, including language/auxiliary-aid protections. See **42 CFR 438.10(d)(3)** in **[42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)**. But the specific NC PDN provider termination steps above come from **3G-1 § 5.2.4.1**.

## Bottom line

For a PDN provider termination, the key NC Medicaid requirement is:

- **Notify NC Medicaid within 5 business days**
- **Submit the DMA-3513 discharge form**
- **Include extra information if another insurer/coverage source is taking over**
- **If the physician ordered the termination, include the physician’s order**

per_question.question: What does federal law define as 'home health services' under Medicaid, and where must they be provided?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under federal Medicaid law, **“home health services”** are the services listed in **42 C.F.R. § 440.70(b)** when they are provided to a beneficiary **at the beneficiary’s place of residence** and under the required practitioner orders and written plan of care. Those services include:

- **Nursing services** provided on a part-time or intermittent basis,
- **Home health aide services,**
- **Medical supplies, equipment, and appliances** suitable for use in settings where normal life activities take place, and
- **Physical therapy, occupational therapy, or speech pathology and audiology services** as an optional home health benefit.  
Cited in [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70.

## Federal rule

The regulation defines home health services as services provided to a beneficiary:

- **At the beneficiary’s place of residence**; and
- **On written orders** from a physician, nurse practitioner, clinical nurse specialist, or physician assistant working in accordance with state law, as part of a **written plan of care** that the ordering practitioner **reviews every 60 days** for nursing, aide, and therapy services; and
- For medical supplies, equipment, and appliances, on the beneficiary’s physician’s orders or orders from another licensed practitioner of the healing arts acting within state-law scope of practice, under a written plan of care.  
See [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70(a).

## Where they must be provided

Federal law says home health services must be provided at the beneficiary’s **“place of residence.”** But the regulation also makes clear what **does not** count as a place of residence for this purpose.

### Excluded settings
A beneficiary’s place of residence **does not include**:

- a **hospital,**
- a **nursing facility,** or
- an **intermediate care facility for individuals with intellectual disabilities (ICF/IID),** except for certain home health services in an ICF/IID that the facility itself is not required to provide.  
See [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70(c).

### Broader place-of-service rule
The regulation further says home health services are **not limited to a private home** or to beneficiaries who are **homebound**. Instead, they may be furnished in **“any setting in which normal life activities take place,”** other than:

- a hospital,
- a nursing facility,
- an ICF/IID, or
- **any setting where Medicaid payment is or could be made for inpatient services that include room and board.**  
See [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70(c)(1).

## Bottom line

Federal Medicaid law defines **home health services** as specified nursing, aide, medical supply/equipment/appliance, and certain therapy services provided under proper practitioner orders and a written plan of care. They must be provided in the beneficiary’s **place of residence**, meaning generally a setting where normal life activities occur, **not** in a hospital, nursing facility, or other inpatient room-and-board setting.  
Source: [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70.

per_question.question: How does NC Medicaid define 'terminally ill' for purposes of hospice eligibility, and what certification is required?
per_question.agent_answer:
For NC Medicaid hospice, a person is **terminally ill** if the required physician certification supports a **life expectancy of six months or less**. The policy text in the certification section repeatedly uses that standard, including for later recertifications, which must explain why the face-to-face clinical findings support a **life expectancy of six months or less**. [[Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment)]

## Required certification

NC Medicaid requires **written certification of terminal illness for each benefit period**. The hospice provider must obtain that written certification **before submitting a claim for payment**. If the written certification cannot be obtained within **two calendar days after a period begins**, an **oral certification** must be obtained within those two days, and the written certification still must be obtained before the claim is submitted. [[Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment)]

### Who must sign it
For the **initial 90-day period**, the hospice must obtain a written certification from:
- the **medical director of the hospice** or the **physician member of the hospice interdisciplinary group (IDG)**; and
- the individual’s **attending physician**, if the individual has one. [[Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment)]

For **subsequent benefit periods**, only certification by the **medical director of the hospice** or the **physician member of the hospice IDG** is required. [[Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment)]

### What the certification must contain
The certification or recertification must include:
- a physician narrative that **briefly synthesizes the clinical information supporting the terminal diagnosis** and attests that the physician composed the narrative after reviewing the clinical information and, when applicable, examining the beneficiary;
- the **election period dates** to which it applies; and
- the certifying or recertifying physician’s **signature and date**. [[Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment)]

For the **third and later benefit period recertifications**, there also must be a **face-to-face encounter** by a hospice physician or hospice nurse practitioner, occurring **before, but no more than 30 calendar days before**, that recertification, to gather clinical findings for continued eligibility. The narrative for those later periods must explain why those findings support a **life expectancy of six months or less**. [[Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment)]

## Timing rules
- Initial certifications may be completed **no more than 15 calendar days before** the effective date of election.
- Recertifications may be completed **no more than 15 calendar days before** the start of the subsequent benefit period. [[Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment)]

**Current source checked for amendments:** Clinical Coverage Policy **3D, Hospice Services**, effective **March 15, 2024**; no separate amending change notice was returned for this document.

per_question.question: What ambulance services are NOT covered by NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid does **not** cover these ambulance services or charges under Clinical Coverage Policy 15:

### Specifically non-covered ambulance services
- An ambulance is called, but **no treatment is needed**
- The ambulance responds to a **false alarm call**
- The beneficiary **refuses all medical services**
- Ambulance transport for a **medical service that is not covered by Medicaid**
- **Commercial airline tickets**
- **Airstrip fees**
- **Taxes** charged separately (local, state, federal, etc.)
- **Separate additional charges for nursing personnel** who are employees of a facility or ambulance service
- **Waiting fees**
- **Separate charges for oxygen, items, and supplies**, because those are included in the base rate
- **Services other than those listed in Section 3.2** of the policy are not covered. [Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment) (Policy 15, § 4.2.1.4, effective 12/15/2023)

### Other ambulance-related limits
NC Medicaid also does not reimburse:
- **Loaded mileage** to a facility that is **not the nearest appropriate facility**  
A hospital is not considered “appropriate” or “inappropriate” based on physician privileges or beneficiary preference. [Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment) (Policy 15, § 4.2.1.1, effective 12/15/2023)

### General non-coverage rules
Even if a service is not listed above, ambulance services are not covered when:
- the beneficiary does **not meet eligibility requirements** in Section 2.0;
- the beneficiary does **not meet the coverage criteria** in Section 3.0;
- the service **duplicates another provider’s service**; or
- the service is **experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial**. [Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment) (Policy 15, § 4.1, effective 12/15/2023)

### Governing coverage rule
The policy ties covered ambulance services to the specific covered criteria in Section 3.2, including emergency services needed to **screen and stabilize** a beneficiary when an emergency medical condition is reasonably believed to exist. per_question.question: Are there quantity limits on prescription drugs under NC Medicaid, and when is prior authorization required for pharmacy claims?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. NC Medicaid policy supports **quantity limits on prescription drugs**, and **prior authorization (PA) is required for some pharmacy claims**, especially for certain high-cost drugs and when claim edits indicate PA is needed.

## Quantity limits

The State Plan says NC Medicaid may establish **“authorizations, limitations, and reviews for specific drugs, drug classes, brands, or quantities”** to manage the pharmacy program. It adds that this **may include limitations on monthly brand-name and generic prescriptions as well as restrictions on the total number of medications**. [State Plan under Title XIX of the Social Security Act Medical Assistance Program](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/documents/medicaid/get-started/state-plan-under-title-xix-social-security-act-medical-assistance-program/open)

The State Plan also says prescribed drugs are covered only within specified program limits and that PA is used for some drugs subject to cost or utilization controls. [State Plan under Title XIX of the Social Security Act Medical Assistance Program](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/documents/medicaid/get-started/state-plan-under-title-xix-social-security-act-medical-assistance-program/open)

In addition, Clinical Coverage Policy 9 refers to **“quantity limitations of episodic drugs”** and **prior authorization criteria and requirements** in outpatient pharmacy administration. [Lock-in Program](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment) (effective 2024-07-15)

per_question.question: Under what conditions can speech therapy be provided via telehealth under NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
Speech therapy may be provided by telehealth under NC Medicaid only in limited circumstances and subject to specific safeguards.

## When telehealth is allowed for speech therapy

NC Medicaid says **a select set of speech and language evaluation and treatment interventions** may be delivered by telehealth. Telehealth may be **medically necessary** when:

- the beneficiary’s medical condition is such that **exposure to others should be avoided**, or
- the beneficiary is in a **remote or underserved location** where access to appropriately qualified providers is limited. [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) (effective 2025-02-01, current), section **e. Telehealth**

## Required conditions

Even when telehealth is available, NC Medicaid requires all of the following:

- **Telehealth must be an adjunct to in-person care, not a replacement**, unless in-person care is contraindicated or unavailable.
- **Telehealth must be in the beneficiary’s best interest**, not just easier for the therapist.
- **Telehealth cannot be used solely to increase therapist productivity.** [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) (effective 2025-02-01, current), section **e. Telehealth**

## Ordinary speech-therapy rules still apply

Using telehealth does **not** remove the underlying speech-language therapy medical-necessity requirements. The service still has to meet the usual **speech-language therapy criteria**, including the policy’s service-specific documentation and clinical standards. [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) (effective 2025-02-01, current), section **3.2.1.3 Speech-Language Therapy (ST)**

## Bottom line

Under NC Medicaid, speech therapy can be provided via telehealth when it is medically necessary for the beneficiary, especially because exposure should be avoided or access to qualified providers is limited, **but** it generally must remain supplemental to in-person care and cannot be used for therapist convenience or productivity. [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

per_question.question: What medical loss ratio (MLR) must Medicaid managed care organizations meet under federal law, and how does NC implement this requirement?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under federal law, Medicaid managed care plans do **not automatically have to meet a national 85% minimum MLR unless the state chooses to impose a minimum**. But every state must require its Medicaid managed care entities to **calculate and report** MLR under the federal formula. If a state does impose a minimum, it must be **at least 85%**. North Carolina does impose a stricter contractual standard: its prepaid health plans (PHPs) must meet a **Department-defined minimum MLR threshold that is 88% in aggregate across all contracted PHPs**, with plan-specific thresholds weighted by each PHP’s capitation revenue mix. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438); [Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

## Federal rule

### 1) What federal law requires
Federal Medicaid managed care rules require the state, through its contracts, to ensure that each MCO, PIHP, and PAHP **calculates and reports** an MLR for each reporting year. If the state elects to require a minimum MLR, that minimum must be **“equal to or higher than 85 percent.”** [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438), § 438.8(a), (c).

So the key federal point is:

- **Reporting/calculation is mandatory**
- **An 85% floor applies only if the state adopts a minimum MLR requirement**
- A state may set a **higher** minimum than 85% [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438), § 438.8(c).

### 2) Federal MLR methodology
Federal law defines MLR as the ratio of:

- **Numerator:** incurred claims + expenditures for activities that improve health care quality + fraud prevention activities [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438), § 438.8(d), (e)(1)
- **Denominator:** adjusted premium revenue, with taxes, licensing, and regulatory fees handled under the federal denominator rules [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438), § 438.8(d), (f)

Federal § 438.8 also specifies major inclusions/exclusions and adjustments, including:

- incurred claims include direct provider payments and certain reserves/liabilities
- overpayment recoveries and prescription drug rebates must be deducted from incurred claims
- non-claims administrative costs are excluded
- a **credibility adjustment** may increase MLR for partially credible plans [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438), § 438.8(d), (e), (h)

### 3) Federal oversight when a state uses a minimum MLR
When a state requires a minimum MLR, the state must annually report to CMS, for each contracted plan, at least:

- numerator amount
- denominator amount
- MLR percentage achieved
- member months
- any remittances owed

If the state requires remittances for failure to meet the minimum MLR, the state must reimburse CMS for the federal share of the remittance. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438), § 438.74(a), (b).

## North Carolina implementation

North Carolina implements the federal MLR requirement in its managed care contract by requiring PHPs to calculate and report MLR annually on **two bases**:

1. **CMS-defined MLR**, calculated as defined in **42 C.F.R. § 438.8**
2. **Department-defined MLR**, which uses a similar framework but with North Carolina-specific adjustments [Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment), “2. Medical Loss Ratio.”

### NC’s CMS-defined MLR
The contract says the PHP must calculate the federal/CMS-defined MLR using:

- numerator = incurred claims + quality improvement expenditures + the lesser of fraud reduction expenditures or fraud reduction recoveries
- denominator = premium revenue minus federal, state, and local taxes and licensing/regulatory fees [Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment), “2. Medical Loss Ratio.”

### NC’s Department-defined MLR
North Carolina also creates a **Department-defined MLR** with specific modifications. The contract allows inclusion of certain **voluntary contributions to health-related resources** if they align with the Department’s Quality Strategy and meet stated community-engagement and beneficiary-improvement conditions. It also excludes certain items, including:

- certain separately reimbursed directed payments
- related-provider payments that violate contract payment limitations
- interest or penalty payments for prompt-pay violations
- certain prior-year rebate-related amounts
- non-claims costs, PBM fees and spread pricing, marketing/branding materials, related-party administrative payments and margin, and administrative costs not allowed as health care quality improvement [Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment), “2. Medical Loss Ratio.”

North Carolina also requires:

- aggregation across all Medicaid eligibility groups covered under the contract
- credibility adjustment for plans with fewer than **380,000 member months**
- compliance with Department MLR templates and instructions [Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment), “2. Medical Loss Ratio.”

### NC’s minimum threshold and consequences
North Carolina’s contract states that:

- the **minimum MLR threshold in aggregate across all contracted PHPs is exactly 88%**
- if a PHP’s **Department-defined MLR** is below the minimum threshold, the PHP must either:
  - remit a rebate to the Department,
  - contribute to approved health-related resources, or
  - split the obligation between those two approaches [Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment), “2. Medical Loss Ratio.”

## Bottom line

- **Federal law:** Medicaid managed care plans must **calculate and report** MLR; if a state imposes a minimum MLR, it must be **at least 85%**. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438), § 438.8
- **North Carolina:** NC goes further and contractually uses an **88% aggregate minimum MLR threshold** for PHPs, with NC-specific Department-defined calculation rules and rebate/contribution consequences if a plan falls short. [Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment), “2. Medical Loss Ratio.”

per_question.question: What are the specific criteria for NC Medicaid coverage of CAR-T cell therapy?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid covers CAR-T cell therapy when the beneficiary meets the policy’s general medical-necessity requirements and the therapy meets the policy’s specific CAR-T criteria. The key specific criteria are:

- The CAR-T therapy must have **U.S. FDA approval**.
- It must be administered **according to the FDA-approved guidelines** for:
  - indications and usage,
  - dosage and administration,
  - dosage forms and strengths, and
  - warnings and precautions.
- It must be administered at a **certified or authorized treatment center**.
- If the particular CAR-T product is subject to an FDA-required **REMS** program, the treatment center must be **enrolled in that REMS**, and providers must be **trained to manage cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and neurologic toxicities**.  
  ([CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 3.2, § 3.2.1, effective 4/1/2025)

In addition, the policy’s general covered-service criteria also apply. The service must be:

- individualized and consistent with the beneficiary’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis,
- safely furnishable, with no equally effective and more conservative or less costly statewide alternative available, and
- furnished in a way not primarily for the convenience of the beneficiary, caregiver, or provider.  
  ([CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 3.1, effective 4/1/2025)

## Important non-coverage limits
NC Medicaid does **not** cover CAR-T therapy if, among other things:

- the product is **not FDA-approved**;
- it is used **outside FDA guidelines** for indications/usage, dosage/administration, or dosage forms/strengths;
- a therapy requiring REMS is given at a facility **not enrolled in that REMS**;
- it is a **repeat CAR-T treatment** for someone who previously received another CAR-T therapy;
- psychosocial history limits the beneficiary’s ability to comply with required pre- and post-infusion care; or
- current beneficiary or caretaker noncompliance makes adherence to the treatment regimen unlikely.  
  ([CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 4.2.1, effective 4/1/2025)

The policy also says CAR-T is not covered if the beneficiary does not meet the policy’s eligibility or coverage criteria, if the service duplicates another provider’s service, or if it is experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial.  
([CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 4.1, effective 4/1/2025)

## Prior approval documentation
For prior approval, the policy requires documentation including:

- a physician-signed letter of medical necessity documenting prior chemotherapy regimens and dates, clinical/social history, and indications for CAR-T;
- verification that the administering facility is a qualified or authorized treatment center;
- recent HIV and hepatitis serologies;
- diagnostic and procedure results, including bone marrow biopsy;
- any other requested diagnostic tests; and
- a complete psychological/social evaluation addressing compliance, support network, post-treatment plan, and relevant mental health, substance use, or legal history.  
  ([CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 5.2.2, effective 4/1/2025)

I checked amendments for Policy 11A-17, and the authoritative current document is the 4/1/2025 version. If you want, I can also turn this into a short prior-authorization checklist for advocates or treating providers.

per_question.question: Can an NC Innovations waiver participant request services that exceed their individual base budget, and what happens if they believe their needs cannot be met within the budget?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. An NC Innovations participant may request services that cost more than the participant’s individual base budget if the participant believes their needs cannot be met within that budget. The policy says the SIS results and the base budget are **guidelines**, not a binding cap, and medically necessary services must be authorized even if they exceed the base budget. If the request is denied, the LME/MCO must explain the reasons and tell the person how to appeal; the participant may also file a grievance about the base budget. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment) (effective Nov. 1, 2016; current per amendment check).

## What the policy says

Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P**, the participant:

- “may request services that cost in excess of his or her base budget if he or she believes his or her needs cannot be met within his or her base budget”; and
- the SIS and base budget “do not constitute a binding limit on the amount of services that may be requested or authorized,” and if the **LME/MCO determines services to be medically necessary, they will be authorized, regardless of the base budget**. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment) (section titled **Category Assignment and Individual Budget Changes**).

## If the participant thinks the budget is not enough

If the participant believes the base budget cannot meet their needs, the policy supports:

- **requesting services above the base budget**;
- submitting supporting information tied to the participant’s needs, including examples in the policy such as behavioral needs that differ from the level description, medical needs that differ from the level description, updated evaluations, behavior support plans, medical records, and certain post-secondary documentation when relevant. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment) (section titled **North Carolina Innovations**).

## What happens if NC Medicaid / the LME-MCO denies the request

If authorization is denied, the policy says the **LME/MCO must notify the individual of**:

- the **reasons** for the decision,
- **how to appeal**, and
- **how to file a grievance regarding the base budget**. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment) (section titled **Category Assignment and Individual Budget Changes**).

## Additional point on very high support needs

For at least one Innovations service context, Policy 8-P also shows that when especially high levels of support are requested, authorization can still occur based on **medical necessity**, and the treatment team should review the person’s status and identify sustainable supports, including options within the waiver and outside it such as Medicaid State Plan services. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment) (section titled **NC Medicaid North Carolina Innovations**).

## Bottom line

The base budget is **not an absolute ceiling**. A participant can ask for more, and if the participant’s needs support medical necessity, services may be authorized above budget. If not approved, the participant should receive a denial reason plus appeal and grievance rights.
